The Climate Threshold

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
New climate research confirms what many experts have long been warning about: the earth might be on an irreversible path to a scorching future. How can humanity prepare for living in a hothouse?

Unique Selling Point:
The Abisko Research Centre is 200km north of the Arctic Circle and provides a unique opportunity to research the effects of global warming on colder climates. Carte Blanche has been offered a unique opportunity to venture to this remote area in the far north of Sweden to speak to some of Europe's leading climate scientists.

Summary:
New research conducted by a group of respected global scientists has found that there exists a climate threshold that, if crossed, would make the effects of climate change irreversible. Worryingly, they suggest, we may already have crossed that line. In other words, even if we cut our greenhouse gas emissions to zero, the impact of the damage already done combined with a number of knock-on effects, means the earth will continue to warm. The net result? A planet that heats up well beyond the 2 degrees set as the limit by global treaties. We will be living in a hothouse.

Among the knock-on effects is the thawing of what's known as the Permafrost - a layer of once continually frozen vegetation found in areas around the poles. Rising temperatures are casing the Permafrost to "unfreeze" releasing carbon di-oxide - previously trapped within frozen vegetation - into the atmosphere. The consequence is what in sporting parlance would be known as a "double whammy": the Permafrost thaws because of higher temperatures, greenhouse gas is emitted as a result, increasing the rate at which atmospheric temperatures rise.

Ellen Dorrepaal is a scientist based at the Abisko Research Centre in the Arctic Circle. She's researching the impact of global warming on the permafrost in a series of fascinating experiments and, crucially, looking at how the impact can be mitigated.

We will spend a day at the centre with Ellen - filming mostly outdoors - as she explains her research, and describes a future shaped by dramatically altered climate.

Further information:
Further input will be gathered from other experts at the centre, and a South African voice will be sought for local context.



Extra Budget Items:
1 x international flight (Dublin to Stockholm)
2 x internal flights (Stockholm to Kiruna)
1 x car hire
2 nights accommodation

Script:


Climate Change Script

VO: It gets cold here. At the height of winter, temperatures plummet to -15 degrees Celsius. Today, it’s late autumn, and the first dustings of snow have arrived. (PAUSE)

VO: But, just three months ago the temperature here reached 30 degrees Celsius. Not that hot by South African standards, but this is Lapland in the Arctic Circle where the average summer temperature is just 17 degrees.

VO: In the Northern Hemisphere summer of 2018, Europe was burning. Close to a hundred people had lost their lives in wildfires that engulfed Attica, in Greece. Vast areas of forest and hundreds of homes had been consumed by flames in one of the most destructive fires of the 21st century.

LINK: Understandably, the deadly fires in Greece captured the world’s attention. But at around about the same time, as many as 80 wildfires were burning in Sweden. And, alarmingly, many of them here in the normally damp Arctic Circle.

VO: While there were no fatalities in the Swedish fires, hundreds of people were evacuated, and thousands of hectares destroyed.

ITV Kevin Winter [18:15:06]: I think there's no doubt that the records are showing us that wildfires are increasing in their frequency and intensity in the northern European countries and also down south as well.

VO: Arguments rage about who or what sparks the fires, but Dr Kevin Winter, like other scientists, is more concerned about what’s providing the fuel. (Strap: Dr Kevin Winter, Future Water Institute, UCT)

ITV Kevin Winter [18:15:06]: Part of that is not because the oxygen levels have changed they've been more or less the same as they were 400 million years ago. What is changing is the biomass is the dead material that is combustible on the earth. In other words, more-and-more dried forest areas that are burning.

LINK: So, was any one of the European wildfires caused by climate change? Well, it’s almost impossible to say. But, here’s what we do know: fires need two things in order to thrive: they need it to be hot and they need it to be dry. And, in 2018, Europe was both of those.

VO: This is an image taken by a NASA satellite in 2017. A year later, the same satellite captured a very different image, one that shows just how much drier Europe had become.

VO: By mid-July this year, temperatures in Scandinavia were 10 degrees Celsius above normal. Small wonder, then, that not even this landscape was spared the flames.

Link: Sweden is also known for its research on the impact of global warming. We’ve travelled from Stockholm in the south of the country to a town called Abisko, about 200km inside the Arctic Circle, to meet someone doing fascinating research on a crucial part of the climate change puzzle.

VO: It’s called Permafrost, a layer of frozen ground beneath the surface found in the upper reaches of the northern hemisphere. Above it, is a much thinner layer of soil known as the active layer because it supports plant and animal life.

VO: Permafrost, on the other hand, is lifeless; a giant freezer storing thousands of years of decayed organic matter. And yet, it has the potential to dictate our future.

VO: And that’s why it’s being closely studied by scientists here at the Abisko Research Station – an institute at the frontline of a warming planet.

VO: One of those scientists is Dr Ellen Dorrepaal (Strap: Dr Ellen Dorrepaal: Plant Ecologist), who’s taking us to a nearby mire or swamp. It’s here that the impact of climate change on the Permafrost is laid bare.

VO: So, why should we care about this soggy field in a far-flung corner of the Arctic Circle? Well, higher temperatures mean the Permafrost is thawing. And that’s bad news because, as it melts the material trapped within it releases more of the greenhouse gasses already responsible for climate change.

LINK: Consider the amount of carbon di-oxide already in the atmosphere, and then double that. Well, that’s the amount trapped in the Permafrost, and it’s also why we at the southern tip of Africa should be paying close attention to what’s happening just under the ground in this part of the world.

ITV: Ellen Dorrepaal [00:01:05]: The big question is how much will come out and how fast will it come up? That's what a lot of the research now is about.

VO: The worst-case scenario would be catastrophic. But, nobody’s predicting that the Permafrost will unleash all its greenhouse gasses. But, what is clear is that small temperature changes can have significant impacts.

ITV: Ellen Dorrepaal [00:04:07]: for example, a study that we did about 10 years ago, we experimentally increased the temperature of a Tundra ecosystem, close by here with only one degree on average temperature in the summer and we found that the emission of co2 from the ecosystem increased by 50 to 60 percent. That's only one degree and already had strong effect.

John Webb [00:05:09] Which does suggest that everybody should be paying close attention to what is happening in permafrost. It should be a cause for concern.

ITV: Ellen Dorrepaal [00:05:20]: It is a global concern because I mean, our atmosphere is pretty well mixed. So, what happens in one part of the world has consequences for climate in another part of the world as well.

VO: And, as if those consequences weren’t concerning enough, thawing Permafrost also releases Methane – a greenhouse gas 84 times more potent than carbon di-oxide. (Pause)

VO: Which begs the question: if we know what and how much is in the ground and that it’s released into the atmosphere when that ground thaws, why the need for all this research?

ITV: Ellen Dorrepaal [00:11:23]: Actually when the permafrost is thawing a lot of nutrients are also released. (CUT) So when you add more nutrients to plants will grow more. Which might balance out some of this carbon dioxide loss that you have from the permafrost soil. Again, the question is how much? What are the drivers of that? (CUT) What does that mean for the carbon uptake? What does it mean for the quality of the new carbon that goes into the soil? All these kinds of questions make it quite complex.

VO: In other words, higher temperatures mean more carbon di oxide and methane. But, they also mean more plant growth. Plants absorb CO2 which - at the very least – will ensure not all the greenhouse gasses make their way into the atmosphere. But, that, is really where the upside ends.

LINK: A recent study tells us that it’s going to be difficult to manage climate change, and that the planet could heat up to 5 degrees higher than pre-industrial times. And, what that means is that by century’s end – perhaps sooner – future generations are going to be living in one giant hot house.

VO: The planet is already a degree warmer than it was around 130 years ago – that’s more-or-less when our greenhouse gas emissions started having an impact. That left us a degree to play with: in other words – if everyone did their part – we could stabilise global warming and limit its impact. This latest study says, hit 2 degrees, and risk a chain reaction that will change the face of the planet forever.

Kevin Winter [18:00:47] Wow. Five degrees is really an extreme. And, of course, it will look like a very different planet to what we currently know and some of the evidence of what we're likely to expect are going to be whole regions that are completely dried out. We certainly won't see the permafrost and the Arctic Circle and ice sheets in the northern and southern hemisphere anymore.

VO: And, less snow and ice at the polls invariably translates to one thing in Southern Africa: drought. More often, and more intense.
Kevin Winter [18:00:47] About a third of our surface water for instance which is fresh water will no longer be available to us.

ITV: Ellen Dorrepaal [00:20:44]: We're at this one minute to 12 moment where we can't say, oh it's the politicians or oh it’s the companies that need to do something. It's all of us. It's our individual choices (CUT) It's our responsibility when we got involved to think about it because it for us, it is for our children, grandchildren, and future generations to come. It’s for us.

VO: 4 or 5 degrees of warming remains a worst-case scenario; there are still too many variables to be certain of anything. But, right now, certainty isn’t our biggest priority – action is. Dr Erik Lundin knows that as well as anybody. (Strap: Dr Erik Lundin, Research Engineer)
He’s been coming to this field for years and has seen it changing in front of his eyes.
John Webb (Reversal) So was it unusually hot this year?

ITV: Erik Lundin [00:14:56] Yeah, it was and even when I talk to people that lived here their whole life to say that this, maybe was the top temperature they ever experienced here. But yeah it's very important to remember that that's not climate but the trend that it gets warmer that is what we call climate and the trend is that it gets warmer. And that's, actually, no question about it.

LINK: Looking at this scenery, as peaceful and serene as it is, it’s hard to imagine that there are invisible forces at play - beneath my feet and in the air around me – irreversibly changing the climate. But, changing it is and the only question is: by how much and at what cost?
Ends.

Rising temperatures are casing the Permafrost to "unfreeze" releasing carbon di-oxide - previously trapped within frozen vegetation - into the atmosphere. The consequence is what in sporting parlance would be known as a "double whammy": the Permafrost thaws because of higher temperatures, greenhouse gas is emitted as a result, increasing the rate at which atmospheric temperatures rise. Ellen Dorrepaal is a scientist based at the Abisko Research Centre in the Arctic Circle. She's researching the impact of global warming on the permafrost in a series of fascinating experiments and, crucially, looking at how the impact can be mitigated. We will spend a day at the centre with Ellen - filming mostly outdoors - as she explains her research, and describes a future shaped by dramatically altered climate.
